1.1 Software Bid

The Enhanced Personal Finance Analyzer is an academic desktop solution for recording personal income and expenditure, planning category budgets, and tracking savings goals. The benefit is a single local view of manually entered financial activity, with immediate explanatory feedback before an expense is recorded. It does not initiate payments or synchronize bank accounts.

The problem is fragmentation of everyday records across cash, digital payment descriptions and informal notes. A monthly total alone does not show which category dominates discretionary spending or how a proposed purchase affects a budget. This project addresses those questions through categorized records, monthly aggregation and transparent financial rules.
Scope of work and technical approach

The final scope includes local account authentication, transaction maintenance, custom categories, monthly category limits, ratio-based savings allocation, recurring-entry catch-up, charts, text reports, and file transfer functions. JavaFX presents forms and tables; Java services apply validation and calculations; JDBC accesses a local SQLite database. Monetary values use BigDecimal in Java and integer paise in storage.

items.caption: Feasibility and deliverables
rows: Java 21, JavaFX, Maven and SQLite are identified in pom.xml and source.
Manual entry and local file persistence suit a single-device demonstration.
Dependencies are available without a paid banking API; no measured project cost is claimed.
Java desktop application, Maven build configuration, source code, automated tests and user-facing financial views.

items.text: The application organizes a financial workflow around tracking, planning and analysis. Tracking creates a categorized history. Planning compares actual spending with monthly limits and records progress toward selected goals. Analysis presents aggregate indicators and rule-triggered observations. The user remains responsible for entering accurate records and deciding how to act on the advice.

Intended users include students and working individuals who want an offline personal ledger rather than a professional accounting system. Each account has its own user identifier. Shared system categories are available to all accounts, while custom categories belong to a particular user. The desktop stores several accounts locally, although only one account is represented by the current in-memory session at a time.
Objectives and boundaries

items.caption: Objectives matched to the final application
rows: Income/Expense model objects; date, category, amount, payment mode and notes.
Category/month budget comparison and 80%/100% alert levels.
Active goals, target amounts, deadlines and percentage allocations.
Recurring rules checked at startup and periodically while running.
Five heuristic rules, category pie chart, three-month bar chart and text report.

items.text: The system does not include bank synchronization, investment portfolios, tax filing, loan management, email delivery, web access or a remote REST backend. An allocation deposit changes goal balances independently of transaction cashflow. A payment mode is a text description, not a connection to a payment provider.
Development approach

The system is organized into functional modules with separate presentation, service, domain and persistence responsibilities. Interface-based DAOs allow storage operations to be implemented independently of most controller code. Existing unit and integration tests check monetary utilities, validation, recommendation rules and selected persistence operations. This modular approach supports focused implementation and verification of individual workflows.

items.caption: Technology stack
rows: 21; compiler source, target and release in Maven.
21.0.5; controls, layouts and charts constructed in Java.
5.10.2; repository unit and integration test sources.

items.text: Desktop architecture

The interface is constructed programmatically with JavaFX controls, layouts and charts. Controllers call Java services through ordinary method calls. DAO interfaces define persistence operations, and JDBC implementations read and write the local SQLite database. TransactionService and RatioAllocationService also contain direct JDBC transactions for expense insertion and goal allocation.
Session and navigation

Registration or sign-in establishes one current local account. MainShellController presents Dashboard, Transactions, Budgets, Savings Goals, Recurring Rules, and Reports & Settings. Navigation callbacks refresh financial views from saved records. Signing out clears the session and returns to the account screen.
Operating constraints

The application requires Java 21, compatible JavaFX native libraries and a writable local working directory. Its relative database path is data/finance.db. Recurring rules are processed while the application runs; startup catch-up handles overdue dates. The application records financial activity manually and does not connect to a bank or initiate payments.
2.1 Use Cases
2.1.1 Use-Case Diagrams

The primary actor is the account holder. Before sign-in, the same person may create an account or submit credentials. After sign-in, the account identifier is passed to the controllers. Diagram boundaries represent the entire local application; SQLite and the recurring scheduler are not external actors.

Recording an entry includes validation; editing also validates the changed data. Deletion is confirmed rather than treated as a validation subcase. Searching and category creation are separate user goals. A successful account registration opens the same application shell as a successful login. The application has no administrator role or password-reset workflow.

items.caption: Planning, automation and analysis use cases

items.text: The planning use cases represent persisted budgets and goals. Creating or activating a goal checks the sum of active allocation ratios. Allocating a deposit is a separate operation; creating income does not automatically allocate savings. Managing a recurring rule configures future ledger generation rather than instructing a bank to debit funds.

Reports, charts and advice read saved records. The advice toggle and fixed-category selection are distinct preferences: disabling advice suppresses all rule messages; marking a category fixed excludes it only from discretionary concentration and category-spike checks. Snapshot creation and restore are exposed functions, but restore is partial and is not a complete account recovery contract.
UC-01  Register, sign in and sign out

items.caption: UC-01 specification
rows: Application initialization completes; local database is reachable.
Select Register & Sign In or Sign In.

1. Enter username and password. 2. Validate registration fields or nonempty login input. 3. Registration checks duplicate username, hashes the password and saves User; login retrieves User and checks BCrypt. 4. Initialize default fixed-category preferences as needed. 5. Set currentUser and open the shell. 6. Sign Out clears currentUser and shows login.

Invalid fields or credentials produce an AuthenticationException message. Duplicate usernames are rejected. Database failures are not comprehensively caught by the login handler, so they remain a reliability risk. Canceling registration mode does not create an account.
A successful operation establishes one in-memory session. Password plaintext is not saved; logout does not delete stored records.

items.text: Registration accepts at least six username characters from letters, digits, underscore, dot and hyphen; demo is a special accepted short name. Password validation requires at least six characters. These are implemented rules, not a recommendation that six-character passwords are sufficient for production security. Account deletion and credential recovery are not user-facing functions.
UC-02  Record income or expense

items.caption: UC-02 specification
rows: Signed in; an appropriate category is available.

1. Choose Income or Expense. 2. Enter amount, category, date, payment mode and optional notes. 3. Observe live preview. 4. Save. 5. UI and service validation run. 6. Income goes through transactionDao.save(); expense uses direct JDBC in addExpense(). 7. Table reloads; dashboard/budgets reload on navigation.

Nonpositive amounts and scale above two decimal places are rejected. Expense dates after today are rejected. SQL insert failure reports an error; addExpense rolls back. Preview does not itself save any data.
A new persisted row has a generated ID, positive stored amount and explicit INCOME/EXPENSE type.

items.text: UC-03  Edit or delete a transaction

items.caption: UC-03 specification
rows: Signed in; selected row belongs to current account.
Double-click row to edit or choose Delete Transaction.
Edit: open populated dialog, keep the type locked, change permitted fields, save and reload. Delete: request deletion, confirm, call deleteTransaction(id,userId), then reload.
Cancel closes without persistence. No selection produces a prompt. Failed updates/deletes may return false or raise a data-access exception.
Successful edit replaces stored values; successful delete removes the selected user-scoped row.

items.text: UC-04  Classify and find financial records

items.caption: UC-04 specification
rows: Add Category or apply Search & Filters.

Create a named category with income/expense type; reject an existing case-insensitive name. For retrieval, specify date range, category, type, amount bounds or notes/category keyword; execute user-scoped query and replace table data. Reset removes filters.

Blank or duplicate category names are rejected. Nonnumeric filter amounts currently become null rather than producing validation feedback. Custom category classification does not alter existing rows automatically.
A saved category becomes selectable; filtered results remain scoped to the account.

items.text: UC-05  Manage monthly category budgets

items.caption: UC-05 specification
rows: Signed in; expense category and month selected.

Enter a positive limit and save. Upsert the unique user/category/month record. Query spending in that category and month. Calculate utilization and show NORMAL, WARNING or EXCEEDED. Edit or delete through the row menu.
Zero/negative limits fail validation. Missing budget gives normal status in the alert service. Overspending is allowed; warnings do not block saving an expense.
A persisted monthly limit and calculated spending comparison are visible.

items.text: UC-06  Create, manage and fund savings goals

items.caption: UC-06 specification
rows: Signed in; current active-goal ratios are available.
Savings Goals > New Savings Goal or Allocate Savings Deposit.

1. Enter title, positive target, deadline and ratio from 0 to 100. 2. Validate fields and active ratio sum. 3. Save a new active goal. 4. Enter a positive deposit. 5. Read active goals and calculate each rounded share. 6. Batch saved_paise increments within one JDBC transaction. 7. Commit and show allocation summary.

Blank titles, nonpositive targets, missing/past deadlines or out-of-range ratios are rejected. The implementation accepts today as a deadline. Exceeding 100% active allocation raises AllocationRatioException. SQL failure rolls back allocation updates. Cancel performs no write.
Goal rows reflect saved allocations. Remainder is returned in the result but has no persisted unallocated-savings account.

items.text: The New/Edit dialog uses a scrollable form and separate action footer. Its size is capped to the current screen bounds after showing. This code change addresses clipping; 100%, 125% and 150% scaling still require manual acceptance checks.
UC-07  Configure and process recurring transactions

items.caption: UC-07 specification
rows: Signed in to create rules; application process running to execute scheduled work.
Create Rule, Run Catch-up Now, startup catch-up or periodic timer.

1. Select type/category, positive amount, frequency and start date; end date is optional. 2. Save ACTIVE rule with nextDueDate=startDate. 3. Find active rules due on/before today. 4. Generate each missed occurrence. 5. Save audit message and advance date with Frequency.nextDate(). 6. Mark expired when the following date exceeds the end date.

End date before start is rejected. Paused rules are skipped until resumed. Processing failure is logged. The current save/audit/advance sequence is not one atomic database transaction, so a mid-sequence failure may cause duplicate retry records.
Transactions carry recurring_rule_id; rule stores its next date/status; execution history records success/failure.

items.caption: Recurring intervals and persisted state
rows: Advance from the current occurrence using plusMonths(1) / plusYears(1).
Persisted RuleStatus enum values. No background service runs when app is closed.

items.text: The manual catch-up command calls the scheduler synchronously from the UI handler. Large backlogs can block interaction; no backlog performance measurement was performed. Automatic periodic callbacks use Platform.runLater to refresh UI tables.
UC-08  Review financial position and preferences

items.caption: UC-08 specification
rows: Signed in; saved records may be empty.
Open Dashboard or refresh monthly report; change advice/fixed preferences.

Read income, expense and category totals. Construct charts and goal snapshot. Build AnalysisContext and evaluate five rules when enabled. Generate monthly text with category/budget/goal summaries. Persist preference changes and refresh insight display after successful advice update.

Zero income avoids division by zero. Disabled advice produces no messages. Individual rule exceptions are logged and do not stop all other rules. Historical micro-spend advice is not strictly aligned to the selected report month.
A read-only analysis is displayed; only explicitly changed preferences are saved.

items.text: UC-09  Transfer financial data through files

items.caption: UC-09 specification
rows: Signed in; suitable file path selected.

Export writes CSV or text; import validates CSV rows and counts imported/skipped records. Backup serializes UserDataSnapshot. Restore reads snapshot and appends selected records to the current account.
Canceling file selection performs no operation. Invalid rows are skipped with reasons. Restore omits recurring rules/preferences, may duplicate records and is not atomic as a whole.
Selected output file exists after successful export; imported records persist where accepted. Restore is only a partial import, not exact recovery.

items.caption: Expense entry with validation and persistence

items.text: The activity starts when the account holder opens a new transaction dialog. The amount and category listeners calculate an advisory preview while the record remains unsaved. Save triggers explicit field parsing and validation. The expense service checks the selected category and rejects an invalid amount or future date.

The expense insertion is protected by setAutoCommit(false), commit and rollback. Generated keys populate the object identifier. Only the success path closes the dialog and refreshes the transaction table. Returning to Dashboard or Budgets calls the navigation refresh callbacks. These activities do not imply a bank transaction or automatic savings-goal deduction.

items.caption: Goal creation followed by ratio allocation

items.text: Goal creation and funding are separate actions. Validation checks the new ratio against the total of currently active goals. A new goal begins active with zero saved amount. A deposit then uses the current active set to calculate shares and applies all saved-balance changes inside a JDBC transaction.

An inactive goal receives no new allocation. The remainder reported to the user is a calculated result, not an account balance in the schema. Independent per-goal rounding can over-allocate tiny deposits; this is a known limitation rather than an omitted decision state. A target being reached is not an automatic transition to inactive: active status is explicitly changed by the user.

items.caption: Responsibilities across user, interface, logic and persistence

items.text: The swimlanes separate responsibility rather than imply remote services. The user supplies information; JavaFX controls collect it; the transaction service enforces validation; JDBC reads categories and inserts the expense. These operations occur in the local process. There is no HTTP request, REST controller, ORM session or server-side deployment.

The JDBC lane includes the expense SQL executed by TransactionService.addExpense(). The service validates the selected category and the financial fields, then commits the insert before recording recent activity. Income creation follows the same domain validation pattern but delegates its save operation to JdbcTransactionDao.
2.3.1 DFD Level 0

items.caption: Context diagram with external entities and data flows

items.text: The context boundary includes authentication, financial records, analytics, scheduled processing and persistence. The external account holder exchanges credentials, entry data, plan settings, queries and preferences with the application. A user-selected file is a separate external source/sink for CSV, report text and serialized snapshots.

DFD notation is data-oriented: rectangles are external entities, circles are transformations, arrows carry named data, and parallel-rule stores appear only in decomposed levels. An arrow is not a method call or execution-order edge. The context diagram deliberately excludes a database actor because SQLite is inside the system boundary.

The aggregated user-input flow is decomposed at Level 1 into credentials, tracking details, planning settings, analysis queries/preferences and file-operation queries. Outputs are decomposed into authentication/operation results, record views, previews, charts/advice and reports. File inputs and outputs retain the same logical content across levels.

Processes 1.0-5.0 divide authentication, tracking, planning, analysis/reporting and file transfer. D1 groups account/preference tables; D2 groups category, transaction and recurring data; D3 groups budgets and savings goals. Repeated symbols identify the same external account holder and logical stores, not extra users or databases.

The same account-holder and file exchanges from Level 0 remain at Level 1. File-operation query is a decomposition of the context query input. Internal report text passes from analysis to transfer for text export. Internal scheduled generation belongs to tracking and is not represented as a new external user input. DFDs describe the implemented data responsibilities, including partial restore; they do not assert atomicity of all process writes.

This diagram expands only process 2.0. Transaction details enter validation, valid entries reach persistence, queries reach retrieval, and category/rule settings reach their management transformation. The D2 interface retains stored-record reads and record-change writes. The external outputs remain operation results and record views.

A validation result is one kind of operation result, not an additional context-level output. The diagram does not add budget-preview inputs to process 2.0 because previews belong to analysis process 4.0 at Level 1. This separation keeps the parent and child interfaces balanced. In the actual UI both responsibilities are combined in the transaction dialog.

title: 2.4 Software Requirement Specification in IEEE Format

items.text: Introduction, purpose and scope

The SRS defines the purpose, operating environment, user characteristics, functional requirements, quality requirements, interfaces and data constraints of the desktop application. Functional requirements are grouped by user goal; acceptance criteria specify observable behavior and connect requirements to use cases and tests.

The product boundary is one JavaFX application process and its local files. Its principal functions are manual ledger management, budget planning, savings allocation, recurring entries and interpretable financial analysis. The account holder supplies financial data and controls local preferences and file operations.

items.caption: Definitions and abbreviations
rows: Data Access Object: an interface/implementation for persistence operations.
Java Database Connectivity API used for SQLite SQL access.
One hundredth of a rupee; integer storage unit.
Integer percentage assigned to an active savings goal.
Per-user classification excluded from discretionary concentration/spike advice.
Explicit threshold rule; not a machine-learned prediction.
Functional requirement / additional requirement / use case / manual test / automated test.

items.text: Overall description

The intended user understands dates, categories and monetary amounts but need not know SQL or Java. Java 21 and JavaFX are required for execution. Maven resolves and launches development builds. The data path is relative to the working directory, so demonstrations should launch from the repository root. The desktop and operating-system clock supply dates and recurring scheduling context.

items.caption: Functional requirements for tracking
rows: Register local accounts, verify BCrypt credentials, establish one session and sign out without deleting data.
Create, view, edit, delete, search and filter account transactions. Amount is positive and scale <=2; expense date is not future. Editing preserves original type.
Offer system/custom categories and category totals. Reject blank or duplicate custom names within visible categories/type.
Set monthly expense-category budgets; calculate spending utilization; show default warning at >=80% and exceeded at >=100%.

items.text: Acceptance boundaries

FR-01 does not include forgotten-password recovery, email verification or server authentication. Usernames accept a restricted character set with a demo exception. Password strength beyond minimum length is not enforced. Financial-data separation primarily relies on user-scoped UI queries and updates; not every DAO lookup takes a user ID.

FR-02 accepts descriptive payment modes, optional notes and date/category/type/amount/keyword filters. Invalid amount-filter text currently disables that bound rather than producing a warning. Future income dates are not rejected by the income validator. Budget warnings are informational; overspending is not blocked.

FR-03 categories have a type and may be system-wide or account-specific. The final interface supports category creation, not a general category editing/deletion screen. FR-04 limits are unique per user/category/month; setting an existing combination updates the limit through SQL upsert.

title: SRS functional requirements for planning and analysis

items.caption: Planning and analysis requirements
rows: Create/edit/delete/toggle goals and distribute positive deposits over active goal ratios. Active total cannot exceed 100 through GoalService.
Persist recurring rules with interval/dates/status; generate due occurrences at startup and configured periodic checks; allow manual catch-up.
Provide an in-modal category budget preview, projected utilization and savings/goal impact before saving.
Allow recommendation preference changes; produce rule advice and monthly text reports with export.

items.text: Calculation and timing semantics

FR-05 deposit allocation is a bookkeeping update to goal balances. It neither checks available net income nor debits an account. Independent rounding is a limitation for tiny deposits. Target completion changes a derived progress value, not a stored lifecycle state.

FR-06 supports DAILY, WEEKLY, MONTHLY and YEARLY. Periodic checks default to five minutes. The process must be running; startup catch-up iterates missed dates. No exactly-once execution guarantee is asserted because transaction insert, audit insert and next-date update are separate operations.

FR-07 is implemented for the current month using an additive proposed amount. A new current-month entry is its reliable intended case. Editing and backdating do not have replacement-aware/date-aware previews. FR-08 report totals use the selected month, but micro-spend advice uses a recent list and today-based window; historical advice therefore has a known period mismatch.

items.caption: Additional functional requirements
rows: Dashboard displays monthly KPIs, category pie chart, a three-month income/expense chart, goals and recent activity. Navigation reloads saved records.
CSV transfer and binary snapshots are exposed. Restore and complex CSV parsing remain partial.
Persist account-specific fixed expense classifications and exclude them from two discretionary rules.
Keep New/Edit Savings Goal controls and action buttons accessible through content sizing, screen-height limits and a scrollable form.

items.caption: Non-functional requirements
rows: Hash passwords; parameterize SQL values; scope financial operations to account.
BCrypt password hashing and prepared SQL statements; local storage is unencrypted.
Protect expense insert and goal-allocation batch with commit/rollback.
Explicit JDBC commit/rollback; recurring execution and restore are not fully atomic.
Readable forms, modal feedback and accessible goal buttons.
JavaFX implementation present; scaling/user study unexecuted.
Interactive entry and bounded background impact are acceptance targets.
No numerical latency or capacity guarantee measured.
Separate UI, services, rules and persistence responsibilities.
Packages/interfaces present; some UI and services use DAOs/SQL directly.
Operate offline while running with local files available.
No network dependency for financial operations; no always-on scheduler.

items.caption: SQLite tables and integrity rules
rows: id PK; username UNIQUE; password_hash; recommendations_enabled; created_at.
id PK; nullable user_id FK for system categories; name; INCOME/EXPENSE; is_system.
id PK; user/category FKs; positive amount_paise; type; txn_date; payment_mode; notes; optional recurring_rule_id; created_at.
id PK; user/category FKs; year_month; positive limit_paise; UNIQUE(user,category,month).
id PK; user FK; title; positive target_paise; nonnegative saved_paise; deadline; ratio 0-100; is_active.

items.text: DatabaseManager enables PRAGMA foreign_keys on each connection. Transaction dates and year-month values are stored as text and selected using an ISO month prefix. User-related rows generally cascade when a user is deleted at DAO level, although the UI does not offer account deletion. Deleting a recurring rule sets existing transaction recurring_rule_id values to NULL and cascades its execution audit rows.

The relational references support one user to many transactions, budgets and goals, and one category to many transactions. A system category may have no owning user. Java domain objects store foreign-key identifiers rather than direct nested User/Category object references. The schema does not encode the cross-row active-ratio total; GoalService enforces it in application logic.

title: SRS interfaces, security and financial logic

items.text: External interface requirements

The user interface is local JavaFX: Login/Register, Dashboard, Transactions, Budgets, Savings Goals, Recurring Rules, and Reports & Settings. Modal dialogs collect transaction, budget, goal, allocation and recurring details. No network protocol or REST interface is required. Software interfaces are JDBC, JavaFX lifecycle/events, BCrypt, Java logging and file streams.

CSV exchange uses Date,Type,Category,Amount,PaymentMode,Notes with ISO dates and decimal rupee amounts. Imports process one line at a time, skip malformed records, and expose imported/skipped counts. Text reports use a file chooser. Binary snapshots use Java object serialization, contain financial data and a User object including its password hash, and are not encrypted.

items.caption: Financial logic and acceptance examples
rows: Income - expense; (income - expense)/income x 100. INR 50,000 and INR 1,100 imply INR 48,900 and 97.8%.
(spent + proposed expense)/limit x 100. INR 1,000 against INR 1,200 implies about 83.33%.
Deposit x ratio/100 rounded to two decimals; 60% of INR 1,000 is INR 600.
Flexible category amount / (all expenses - fixed expenses); trigger strictly above 40%.
Expense/income >90%; net savings/income <10%; category growth >=25% with prior >=INR 500; >=5 expenses below INR 200.

items.text: The local SQLite database and serialized snapshots are unencrypted. Snapshots include a User object and its password hash, so access depends on operating-system file permissions. Snapshot deserialization is suitable only for trusted local files. Account authentication uses BCrypt; password recovery and remote roles are outside the application scope.

HeuristicEngine evaluates five independent Recommendation implementations against an AnalysisContext. Each rule returns Optional<String>: a present value is displayed as advice; an empty value indicates that the rule has not triggered. The account preference can suppress the complete recommendation list.

items.caption: Financial recommendation rules
rows: Fixed-category expenses are removed from the denominator and excluded as candidates.
Warns when the monthly expense burden approaches income; zero income is handled separately.
Compares category spending with the preceding month; fixed categories are excluded.
Uses income minus expenses rather than savings-goal deposits.
At least 5 expenses below INR 200 in the recent window
Uses the supplied recent transaction list and today-based date window.

items.text: Preference handling

CategoryService supplies account-specific fixed-category identifiers. The engine enriches the analysis context before iterating over rules. ReportsSettingsController persists recommendation preference changes through AuthService and invokes the dashboard insight callback after a successful update.
Failure handling and analytical limits

An exception in one rule is logged without preventing the remaining rules from running. Advice is explanatory and does not block a transaction. Monthly totals are selected by report month, while the micro-transaction rule uses a bounded recent list and a today-based window; its advice can therefore differ from a historical-month interpretation.

title: Financial Data Integrity and Business Constraints

items.caption: Domain constraints and enforcement
rows: Positive transaction amounts with at most two decimal places
Validators checks input; MoneyUtil converts decimal rupees to integer paise.
validateExpense rejects a future expense date.
A selected category must exist and match the transaction type
TransactionService validates category identity/type before persistence.
One positive limit per account, category and month
BudgetService validates; a unique database constraint supports upsert.
Active allocation percentages total at most 100
GoalService checks creation, active updates and reactivation.
Only active goals receive deposit shares
RatioAllocationService reads active goals and batches saved_paise updates.
End date cannot precede start date
Rule validation checks dates; scheduler advances due dates using frequency.

items.text: Persistence transaction boundaries

Expense insertion runs with auto-commit disabled and commits after generated-key retrieval. On SQL failure it rolls back. Savings allocation also batches balance updates within one JDBC transaction. Fixed-category replacement deletes and inserts account preferences within a transaction, so an invalid category rolls back the replacement.
Known system constraints

Recurring occurrence insertion, audit logging and next-date advancement are separate operations. Snapshot restoration appends selected records and omits recurring rules and fixed-category preferences. Independent rounding of very small goal allocations can exceed the original deposit. These limits affect recovery and edge-case behavior and do not represent additional persisted states.

items.caption: Requirements to use cases, implementation and tests

items.text: The matrix connects user requirements to principal use cases and implementation modules. Automated cases A01–A28 record executed assertions; cases T01–T20 cover screen interaction and additional acceptance scenarios. An automated result applies to its asserted service behavior, not to the entire associated graphical workflow.

3.1 Class Diagram
Case 1 Transaction management

items.caption: Actual transaction classes, interfaces and dependencies

items.text: Income and Expense inherit the shared identifiers, amount, date and descriptive fields of abstract Transaction. Their getType() and getSignedAmount() methods supply dynamic behavior. JdbcTransactionDao realizes TransactionDao, whose generic parent contract is Dao<Transaction,Long>. Dashed dependencies indicate service use or object construction, not ownership.

Multiplicity between Transaction and Category is a relational identifier reference: each saved transaction has one category_id and a category may classify many transactions. It is not a Java field of type Category. TransactionService validates category existence before saving. Its expense path contains direct JDBC SQL, while its income path calls the DAO interface. The diagram therefore shows both object creation and persistence abstraction without claiming uniform delegation.

BudgetService creates monthly Budget objects and delegates storage to BudgetDao. GoalService creates and validates SavingsGoal objects using SavingsGoalDao. RatioAllocationService reads active goals through that interface but executes its allocation batch directly using DatabaseManager. That direct SQL dependency is explained in the component model.

The userId fields represent one account to many budgets or goals through foreign keys. User is omitted from this focused service view; no owning List<Budget> or List<SavingsGoal> is present in that Java model. The stored active flag is separate from progress. A goal remains active after reaching its target unless explicitly deactivated. Dashed dependencies indicate service use, not ownership.
Model and service responsibilities

SavingsGoal stores the target, saved amount, deadline, allocation percentage and active flag. Its progress method calculates a display value from savedAmount and targetAmount. GoalService.getTotalActiveRatio() iterates over active goals; createGoal(), updateGoal() and toggleGoalActive() use this total to protect the allocation pool. RatioAllocationService uses the same active-goal set when distributing an entered deposit.

Budget stores a category, month and limit. BudgetService combines this plan with transaction totals to calculate utilization. There is no Java ownership collection linking a Budget to transactions: the service joins their meaning through account, category and month identifiers. The DAO interfaces isolate ordinary save and lookup operations, while allocation uses a direct JDBC transaction for its batch update.
Case 1 Adding an expense

items.caption: Expense validation and JDBC commit sequence

items.text: TransactionDialogController invokes TransactionService.addExpense(). The service obtains the category through JdbcCategoryDao and calls Validators.validateExpense(). The JDBC participant groups connection, statement and database interactions. The success path returns an Expense with its generated identifier.

On SQLException the insert path calls rollback() and throws DataAccessException; the dialog catches the exception and keeps the form available. The success result is an Expense with its generated ID. TransactionsController then re-queries the table. Preview queries occur before this save sequence and do not commit a record. The expense path executes SQL directly in addExpense(); income persistence uses the transaction DAO.
Case 2 Creating a savings goal

items.caption: Goal validation, ratio check and insertion

items.text: GoalService validates the proposed fields, reads all active goals and sums allocation ratios before insertion. If the total plus the new ratio exceeds 100, AllocationRatioException is raised before save(). JdbcSavingsGoalDao binds values to INSERT savings_goals and returns the object with a generated identifier.

The sequence documents creation only. Funding is a later RatioAllocationService operation, not a side effect of createGoal(). Validation and the sum check are application operations; they are not a database-wide cross-row constraint or a proven concurrent transaction guarantee. The dialog catches ratio errors separately and presents a targeted warning.
Case 1 Transaction persistence

This communication diagram emphasizes object links and numbered messages rather than time-scaled lifelines. Message 1 starts the use case, 1.1 obtains category information, 1.2 validates fields, and 1.3-1.6 perform transactional JDBC work. The dashed return completes the Expense result.

The local JDBC Connection and database are represented separately to expose the persistence boundary. prepareStatement() creates a PreparedStatement, which is abbreviated into the connection interaction to avoid overcrowding. executeUpdate() inserts one row; generated-key retrieval assigns the ID. The commit/rollback label represents alternative outcomes and does not imply both execute on success.

Income persistence uses transactionDao.save() instead of the direct expense SQL path. The collaboration is intentionally limited to one significant actual scenario rather than merging incompatible alternatives into a single call chain.
Case 2 Financial recommendation generation

DashboardController queries current and previous spending before passing AnalysisContext to HeuristicEngine. The engine checks the user preference, obtains account-specific fixed-category information through CategoryService, and creates an enriched context using withFixedCategoryData(). It iterates over five Recommendation implementations and collects present Optional<String> messages.

HighCategorySpendRule and CategorySpikeRule skip fixed categories. Total-expense and savings-rate rules still include fixed obligations. The communication therefore supports explainable advice without suggesting a machine-learning model or external recommendation service.

Recommendation defines evaluate(AnalysisContext) and getRuleName(). Concrete rules implement both methods. The collection List<Recommendation> allows the engine to invoke different financial checks through the same interface.
Case 1 Transaction dialog lifecycle

These are conceptual UI workflow states, not values stored in transactions. A new form permits a type choice; an edit form starts from an existing object and disables type controls. Both enter validation on Save. Invalid input or an SQL error leaves the dialog available for correction.

Successful persistence closes the dialog and returns the saved record. Cancel closes it without a persistence call. Dialog workflow states are not stored in the transactions table. Editing an existing object can change its in-memory values before a failed update, while saved database values change only when persistence succeeds.
Case 2 Persisted active status of a goal

The stored state distinction is is_active=1 or is_active=0. A valid creation starts active. Deactivation removes the goal from future allocation; reactivation checks whether its ratio fits within the current active pool. Deletion removes the row rather than changing a status to DELETED.

Funding changes saved_paise while retaining the active flag. Reaching the target does not automatically deactivate a goal. getProgressPercentage() derives a percentage and caps its display at 100. A deadline passing is not an implemented EXPIRED transition for SavingsGoal. Recurring rules have a separate ACTIVE/PAUSED/EXPIRED enumeration and must not be confused with goal states.
4.1 Component Diagrams

MainApp constructs DAOs, services, file managers and controllers using constructor injection. JavaFX controllers combine view building and event handling. Services implement business rules, while JDBC DAOs map rows to models. HeuristicEngine coordinates the independent Recommendation implementations. RecurringScheduler owns a single-thread scheduled executor.

Controllers coordinate screens and events, services enforce financial rules, and DAOs map persisted records. DashboardController also performs direct DAO queries, while TransactionService.addExpense() and RatioAllocationService.allocateDeposit() contain SQL transactions. MainApp wires dependencies and file-operation callbacks; stop() shuts down the scheduler and logger.

Java language mechanisms include abstract classes, interfaces, overriding, overloaded constructors/methods, generic DAOs, collections, lambdas, streams, try-with-resources and checked/unchecked exceptions. Transaction.getSignedAmount() is overridden by Income and Expense; AnalysisContext.isFixed(long/String) is an actual overload.

The executable environment is a local Java 21 JVM with JavaFX and JDBC libraries. Maven is a build/launch tool, not a hosted runtime service. The application accesses data/finance.db through a local SQLite JDBC URL and loads app.properties/style.css as resources. File choosers write CSV, text and snapshots to user-selected paths.
Execution and local storage

Maven compiles and launches the Java application with its configured dependencies. JavaFX native libraries must match the operating system. Configuration and CSS are packaged resources; the SQLite database, application logs and user-selected CSV, text and snapshot files remain local. Changing the working directory changes the location resolved by the relative database URL.

items.text: 5.1 Test Plan

Testing checks financial validation, monetary calculations, recommendation rules and selected database workflows. The execution on 16 November 2026 compiled all 85 production Java files and 8 test source files using Java 21. All 28 existing @Test methods passed under the JUnit Jupiter engine. Lifecycle methods were executed by the engine. Database tests used a new disposable SQLite file with isolated configuration.

items.caption: Test environment and strategy
rows: Windows; Java 21; JavaFX 21.0.5; JUnit Jupiter 5.10.2; cached project dependencies.
Temporary compiled classes and app.properties; unique SQLite test file; application database unchanged.
Money conversion/aggregation, username/password/amount/date validation, five recommendation rules and preference suppression.
Transaction creation/validation, category duplicates, budget save/query and alert levels, goal ratio cap, deposit balances, fixed-category rollback and account isolation.
Authentication screens, edit/delete, charts, navigation refresh, recurring scheduling, file exchange and display scaling.
Sources compile; test resources point to a disposable database; required libraries available.
Automated assertions pass; manual acceptance results recorded; critical defects resolved before operational acceptance.

items.text: Boundary-value and equivalence-class testing cover positive and invalid monetary inputs, future expense dates, budget utilization classes and the active savings ratio cap. The budget test samples 50%, 85% and 105%; exact 80% and 100% boundaries remain manual acceptance cases. The allocation test verifies a successful update and reloaded balances, not an induced rollback failure.

GUI, performance, security and display-scaling checks are pending manual verification. The complete existing automated suite passed, but this does not establish screen usability, CSV round-trip reliability or complete snapshot recovery. The equal-share concentration test has an order-sensitive assertion and remains a portability risk.
Executed on 16 November 2026. Pass means the assertions in the named existing test method completed successfully.
